---
topic: [Programming]
subtopic: [NET]
summary: "Filters around ASP.NET Core Web API controller actions and endpoint-handler invocations."
level: ["2"]
priority: Medium
status: Ready to Repeat
publish: true
qard-deck: "Programming"
qard-topic: "NET/ASP NET Web API/Filters"
flashcard_uid: "ef27222b"
created: "2026-02-19T23:08:30.000Z"
modified: "2026-11-02T09:03:54.806Z"
---

Controller filters in ASP.NET Core Web APIs wrap defined stages of controller execution. They fit cross-cutting behavior that needs action arguments, model state, controller metadata, or the action result. A correlation-ID rule tied only to selected controllers is one example. An application-wide correlation ID usually belongs in middleware.

The filter APIs live in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc`, but they also apply to [Web API controllers derived from `ControllerBase`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/web-api/?view=aspnetcore-10.0); rendering views is not required. Minimal API handlers use endpoint filters, which have a different invocation context. Endpoint filters can also be [explicitly attached to mapped controller actions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/min-api-filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0#register-a-filter-on-controller-actions).

The boundary matters. Middleware can cover every request type but lacks controller action context. Endpoint code has full local context but duplicates a rule when many actions need it. Filters occupy the space between those two.

Controller filters run after routing has selected a controller action.

- Authorization filters run first and can short-circuit unauthorized requests.
- Resource filters run around most of the rest of the pipeline and can short-circuit early.
- Action filters run before and after the action method.
- Exception filters observe unhandled exceptions from action execution.
- Result filters run before and after the action result is executed.

Scope and filter type both affect nesting. `IOrderedFilter.Order` can override the default scope order, so a custom order should be treated as part of the endpoint's behavior.

# Example

This async action filter rejects selected requests without a correlation header:

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Filters;

public sealed class RequireCorrelationIdFilter : IAsyncActionFilter
{
    public async Task OnActionExecutionAsync(
        ActionExecutingContext context,
        ActionExecutionDelegate next)
    {
        if (!context.HttpContext.Request.Headers.ContainsKey("X-Correlation-Id"))
        {
            context.Result = new BadRequestObjectResult(new
            {
                error = "X-Correlation-Id header is required"
            });
            return;
        }

        await next();
    }
}

// Program.cs
builder.Services.AddScoped<RequireCorrelationIdFilter>();

builder.Services.AddControllers(options =>
{
    // Global registration
    options.Filters.AddService<RequireCorrelationIdFilter>();
});
```

For one action or controller, `[ServiceFilter(typeof(RequireCorrelationIdFilter))]` applies the registered filter without making it global.

An exception filter can translate an unhandled exception from action execution into an API error result:

```csharp
public sealed class ApiExceptionFilter(ILogger<ApiExceptionFilter> logger) : IAsyncExceptionFilter
{
    public Task OnExceptionAsync(ExceptionContext context)
    {
        logger.LogError(context.Exception, "Unhandled exception in {Action}",
            context.ActionDescriptor.DisplayName);

        context.Result = context.Exception is NotFoundException
            ? new NotFoundObjectResult(new { error = context.Exception.Message })
            : new ObjectResult(new { error = "An unexpected error occurred." }) { StatusCode = 500 };

        context.ExceptionHandled = true;
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```

Global registration applies it to every controller action: `builder.Services.AddControllers(opts => opts.Filters.Add<ApiExceptionFilter>());`. Middleware remains the broader choice when errors from routing or Minimal API handlers need the same response contract.

# Applying Filters: `[ServiceFilter]` Vs `[TypeFilter]` Vs `IFilterFactory`

Attributes cannot receive runtime services through their own constructors, so attachment determines how the real filter instance is created.

- **`[ServiceFilter(typeof(MyFilter))]`** resolves the filter itself from DI, so `MyFilter` must be registered with the intended lifetime.
- **`[TypeFilter(typeof(MyFilter))]`** uses `ActivatorUtilities`. Constructor services come from DI, while `Arguments` can supply literal values. The filter type itself does not need registration.
- **`IFilterFactory`** gives an attribute explicit control over creation of the executable filter and whether the result can be reused.
- A plain filter attribute can carry literal metadata but cannot accept runtime services in its attribute constructor.

`[Authorize]` contributes authorization metadata. Under default endpoint routing, authorization middleware enforces that metadata before the controller endpoint runs. Duplicating policy checks in an action filter creates two access-control paths. Within a filter type, the usual nesting is global, controller, then action on the way in and the reverse on the way out. If a filter implements both sync and async forms of the same stage, the runtime invokes only the async interface. The filter's synchronous methods then run only when that async implementation calls them, as the default async methods of `ActionFilterAttribute` do, so custom filter logic belongs in one form per stage.

# Pitfalls

- **Blocking I/O:** `.Result` or synchronous remote calls hold request threads while no CPU work is happening. I/O-bound filters should implement the async interface and await the operation.
- **Authorization in action filters:** a second permission system drifts away from registered policies. Access decisions belong in authentication handlers and authorization policies.
- **Treating exception filters as global error handling:** exception filters cover unhandled exceptions from controller creation, model binding, action filters, and action methods. They do not cover middleware, routing, resource filters, result filters, or action-result execution. Exception-handling middleware is the safer outer boundary for a uniform API error contract.

# Tradeoffs

| Option | Best for | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Middleware | App-wide cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth, exception handling) | No direct controller action context |
| Controller filters | Concerns tied to Web API controllers/actions and model/action context | Their stages do not apply to Minimal API handlers |
| Endpoint filters | Minimal API handler behavior, or explicit attachment to mapped controller actions | Invocation context differs from controller model-state and action-result context |

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: b5d3f2ba-51a2-4fd2-9508-aa0de30ad608 -->
> [!qard]- In an ASP.NET Core controller-based Web API, what is the normal order of filter stages?
> After routing selects a controller action, the filter stages run in this order: authorization, resource, action, then result. Exception filters are not a sequential stage; they run only when an unhandled exception occurs.
>
> 1. **Authorization filters** run first and can short-circuit an unauthorized request.
> 2. **Resource filters** run their before logic next, ahead of model binding, and their after logic last, once the rest of the pipeline has completed.
> 3. **Action filters** run immediately before and after the action method.
> 4. **Result filters** run immediately before and after the action result executes.
> 
> Full flow: authorization → resource (before) → action (before) → action method → action (after) → result (before) → result execution → result (after) → resource (after).
>
> Action filters finish before result filters start, so an action filter's after logic can still replace the result. Only resource filters wrap both the action and the result stages.
>
> These are controller-filter stages. Minimal API handlers use endpoint filters rather than this staged controller pipeline.
>
> [Microsoft: Filters in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0)
<!-- qard-id: ec8874e5-0ca6-4d53-a3dd-6594e0a512e3 -->
> [!qard]- Which exceptions can controller exception filters handle in an ASP.NET Core Web API?
> Controller exception filters handle only unhandled exceptions raised during controller creation, model binding, action filters or the action method. They are not a before-and-after stage; they run only when such an exception occurs.
>
> **Not covered:**
>
> - Exceptions from authorization filters and resource filters, which run outside that part of the pipeline.
> - Exceptions from result filters or from executing the action result.
> - Exceptions from middleware, routing or Minimal API handlers, which run outside the controller-filter pipeline.
>
>
> [Microsoft: Filters in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0)

> [!qard]- What happens after an ASP.NET Core controller exception filter handles an exception?
> - **Handled:** the filter sets `ExceptionHandled` to `true` or assigns a `Result`, and the exception stops propagating. A supplied `Result` is executed as the response. Ordinary result filters do not run around it; only always-run result filters, such as `IAlwaysRunResultFilter` implementations, do.
> - **Not handled:** the exception leaves the controller-filter pipeline and continues to outer middleware, such as exception-handling middleware.
> 
> Because of these gaps, exception-handling middleware is the broader boundary for a uniform API error response.
>
> [Microsoft: Filters in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0)
<!-- qard-id: b115f4c1-4ffb-413c-917b-d5fcdb62cb05 -->
> [!qard]- Within one ASP.NET Core Web API controller-filter type, how do scope and the `Order` property determine execution order?
> By default, scope decides the order among filters of one type: global filters wrap controller filters, which wrap action filters. An explicit `Order` value, exposed through `IOrderedFilter`, takes precedence over scope.
>
> - **Equal `Order` values:** before logic runs global → controller → action, and after logic runs action → controller → global.
> - **Different `Order` values:** filters are sorted by `Order` first and by scope second. A lower value runs its before logic earlier and its after logic later, so it wraps filters with higher values regardless of their scope.
> 
> For example, an action-level action filter with `Order` 0 runs its before logic ahead of a global action filter with `Order` 1.
>
> This ordering only arranges filters of the same type. It cannot move an action filter ahead of an authorization filter, because each filter type runs at its own stage of the controller pipeline.
>
> [Microsoft: Filters in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0)

# References

- [Filters in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0)

> [!qard]- Which exceptions can controller exception filters handle in an ASP.NET Core Web API?
> Controller exception filters handle only unhandled exceptions raised during controller creation, model binding, action filters or the action method. They are not a before-and-after stage; they run only when such an exception occurs.

> **Not covered:**
>
> - Exceptions from authorization filters and resource filters, which run outside that part of the pipeline.
> - Exceptions from result filters or from executing the action result.
> - Exceptions from middleware, routing or Minimal API handlers, which run outside the controller-filter pipeline.
>

Ordinary result filters do not run around it; only always-run result filters, such as `IAlwaysRunResultFilter` implementations, do.
> - **Not handled:** the exception leaves the controller-filter pipeline and continues to outer middleware, such as exception-handling middleware.
>

>

> [!qard]- Within one ASP.NET Core Web API controller-filter type, how do scope and the `Order` property determine execution order?
> By default, scope decides the order among filters of one type: global filters wrap controller filters, which wrap action filters. An explicit `Order` value, exposed through `IOrderedFilter`, takes precedence over scope.
>
> - **Equal `Order` values:** before logic runs global → controller → action, and after logic runs action → controller → global.

---
topic: [Programming]
subtopic: [NET]
summary: "Filters around ASP.NET Core Web API controller actions and endpoint-handler invocations."
level: ["2"]
priority: Medium
status: Ready to Repeat
publish: true
qard-deck: "Programming"
qard-topic: "NET/ASP NET Web API/Filters"
flashcard_uid: "ef27222b"
created: "2026-02-19T23:08:30.000Z"
modified: "2026-11-02T09:03:54.806Z"
---

Controller filters in ASP.NET Core Web APIs wrap defined stages of controller execution. They fit cross-cutting behavior that needs action arguments, model state, controller metadata, or the action result. A correlation-ID rule tied only to selected controllers is one example. An application-wide correlation ID usually belongs in middleware.

The filter APIs live in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc`, but they also apply to [Web API controllers derived from `ControllerBase`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/web-api/?view=aspnetcore-10.0); rendering views is not required. Minimal API handlers use endpoint filters, which have a different invocation context. Endpoint filters can also be [explicitly attached to mapped controller actions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/min-api-filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0#register-a-filter-on-controller-actions).

The boundary matters. Middleware can cover every request type but lacks controller action context. Endpoint code has full local context but duplicates a rule when many actions need it. Filters occupy the space between those two.

Controller filters run after routing has selected a controller action.

- Authorization filters run first and can short-circuit unauthorized requests.
- Resource filters run around most of the rest of the pipeline and can short-circuit early.
- Action filters run before and after the action method.
- Exception filters observe unhandled exceptions from action execution.
- Result filters run before and after the action result is executed.

Scope and filter type both affect nesting. `IOrderedFilter.Order` can override the default scope order, so a custom order should be treated as part of the endpoint's behavior.

# Example

This async action filter rejects selected requests without a correlation header:

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Filters;

public sealed class RequireCorrelationIdFilter : IAsyncActionFilter
{
    public async Task OnActionExecutionAsync(
        ActionExecutingContext context,
        ActionExecutionDelegate next)
    {
        if (!context.HttpContext.Request.Headers.ContainsKey("X-Correlation-Id"))
        {
            context.Result = new BadRequestObjectResult(new
            {
                error = "X-Correlation-Id header is required"
            });
            return;
        }

        await next();
    }
}

// Program.cs
builder.Services.AddScoped<RequireCorrelationIdFilter>();

builder.Services.AddControllers(options =>
{
    // Global registration
    options.Filters.AddService<RequireCorrelationIdFilter>();
});
```

For one action or controller, `[ServiceFilter(typeof(RequireCorrelationIdFilter))]` applies the registered filter without making it global.

An exception filter can translate an unhandled exception from action execution into an API error result:

```csharp
public sealed class ApiExceptionFilter(ILogger<ApiExceptionFilter> logger) : IAsyncExceptionFilter
{
    public Task OnExceptionAsync(ExceptionContext context)
    {
        logger.LogError(context.Exception, "Unhandled exception in {Action}",
            context.ActionDescriptor.DisplayName);

        context.Result = context.Exception is NotFoundException
            ? new NotFoundObjectResult(new { error = context.Exception.Message })
            : new ObjectResult(new { error = "An unexpected error occurred." }) { StatusCode = 500 };

        context.ExceptionHandled = true;
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```

Global registration applies it to every controller action: `builder.Services.AddControllers(opts => opts.Filters.Add<ApiExceptionFilter>());`. Middleware remains the broader choice when errors from routing or Minimal API handlers need the same response contract.

# Applying Filters: `[ServiceFilter]` Vs `[TypeFilter]` Vs `IFilterFactory`

Attributes cannot receive runtime services through their own constructors, so attachment determines how the real filter instance is created.

- **`[ServiceFilter(typeof(MyFilter))]`** resolves the filter itself from DI, so `MyFilter` must be registered with the intended lifetime.
- **`[TypeFilter(typeof(MyFilter))]`** uses `ActivatorUtilities`. Constructor services come from DI, while `Arguments` can supply literal values. The filter type itself does not need registration.
- **`IFilterFactory`** gives an attribute explicit control over creation of the executable filter and whether the result can be reused.
- A plain filter attribute can carry literal metadata but cannot accept runtime services in its attribute constructor.

`[Authorize]` contributes authorization metadata. Under default endpoint routing, authorization middleware enforces that metadata before the controller endpoint runs. Duplicating policy checks in an action filter creates two access-control paths. Within a filter type, the usual nesting is global, controller, then action on the way in and the reverse on the way out. If a filter implements both sync and async forms of the same stage, the runtime invokes only the async interface. The filter's synchronous methods then run only when that async implementation calls them, as the default async methods of `ActionFilterAttribute` do, so custom filter logic belongs in one form per stage.

# Pitfalls

- **Blocking I/O:** `.Result` or synchronous remote calls hold request threads while no CPU work is happening. I/O-bound filters should implement the async interface and await the operation.
- **Authorization in action filters:** a second permission system drifts away from registered policies. Access decisions belong in authentication handlers and authorization policies.
- **Treating exception filters as global error handling:** exception filters cover unhandled exceptions from controller creation, model binding, action filters, and action methods. They do not cover middleware, routing, resource filters, result filters, or action-result execution. Exception-handling middleware is the safer outer boundary for a uniform API error contract.

# Tradeoffs

| Option | Best for | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Middleware | App-wide cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth, exception handling) | No direct controller action context |
| Controller filters | Concerns tied to Web API controllers/actions and model/action context | Their stages do not apply to Minimal API handlers |
| Endpoint filters | Minimal API handler behavior, or explicit attachment to mapped controller actions | Invocation context differs from controller model-state and action-result context |

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: b5d3f2ba-51a2-4fd2-9508-aa0de30ad608 -->
> [!qard]- In an ASP.NET Core controller-based Web API, what is the normal order of filter stages?
> After routing selects a controller action, the filter stages run in this order: authorization, resource, action, then result. Exception filters are not a sequential stage; they run only when an unhandled exception occurs.
>
> 1. **Authorization filters** run first and can short-circuit an unauthorized request.
> 2. **Resource filters** run their before logic next, ahead of model binding, and their after logic last, once the rest of the pipeline has completed.
> 3. **Action filters** run immediately before and after the action method.
> 4. **Result filters** run immediately before and after the action result executes.
> 
> Full flow: authorization → resource (before) → action (before) → action method → action (after) → result (before) → result execution → result (after) → resource (after).
>
> Action filters finish before result filters start, so an action filter's after logic can still replace the result. Only resource filters wrap both the action and the result stages.
>
> These are controller-filter stages. Minimal API handlers use endpoint filters rather than this staged controller pipeline.
>
> [Microsoft: Filters in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0)

> - Exceptions from result filters or from executing the action result.
> - Exceptions from middleware, routing or Minimal API handlers, which run outside the controller-filter pipeline.
>

Ordinary result filters do not run around it; only always-run result filters, such as `IAlwaysRunResultFilter` implementations, do.
> - **Not handled:** the exception leaves the controller-filter pipeline and continues to outer middleware, such as exception-handling middleware.
>

>
> [Microsoft: Filters in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/mvc/controllers/filters?view=aspnetcore-10.0)

---
topic: [Programming]
subtopic: [NET]
summary: "C#'s unit of behavior, covering parameter modifiers and dispatch keywords."
level: ["4"]
priority: Medium
status: Ready to Repeat
publish: true
qard-deck: "Programming"
qard-topic: "NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Methods"
flashcard_uid: "a3e803d0"
created: "2026-02-15T16:27:13.000Z"
modified: "2026-11-03T19:50:44.499Z"
published: "2026-07-08T13:14:17.325Z"
---

Methods define where behavior begins and what data may cross the boundary. The parameter list is part of that contract. By-value parameters isolate the caller's variable, `ref` and `out` expose it for reassignment, and `in` exposes storage as readonly. `params` changes how an expanded argument list is collected at the call site.

Inheritance adds a separate question: which implementation runs? `virtual` and `override` use runtime dispatch. `new` hides a member and leaves selection to the compile-time type of the reference. Similar syntax, very different behavior.

# Input Parameters

## Ref

`ref` aliases the caller's storage rather than copying its current value into a new parameter variable.

- The caller must initialize the variable.
- The method can read and write the variable.

For reference types, `ref` allows the callee to replace the caller's reference rather than only mutate the referenced object:

```csharp
class MyClass {}

static void ModifyReference(ref MyClass obj)
{
    obj = new MyClass();
}

var myObj = new MyClass();
ModifyReference(ref myObj);
```

For value types, `ref` allows the callee to update the caller's variable:

```csharp
static void InitializeAndModify(ref int value)
{
    value = 10;
}

int num = 0;
InitializeAndModify(ref num);
```

## In

`in` is a readonly by-reference parameter. It can avoid copying a large struct, though the compiler may still create a temporary for argument expressions that are not variables.

- The caller must initialize the argument.
- The method can read, but cannot assign to the parameter.
- It is most useful when measurements show that copying a large readonly struct matters.

```csharp
static void ProcessData(in int value)
{
    // value = 10; // Compile-time error
    Console.WriteLine(value);
}
```

## Out

`out` also aliases caller storage, but the value flows outward. The caller need not initialize it, and every normal return path must assign it. This supports `Try*` APIs that separate success from the produced value.

```csharp
static bool TryDivide(int a, int b, out int result)
{
    if (b == 0) { result = 0; return false; }
    result = a / b;
    return true;
}

if (TryDivide(10, 2, out var quotient))   // 'quotient' declared inline
    Console.WriteLine(quotient);           // 5
```

`Dictionary.TryGetValue` shows the boundary well: a missing key is expected input, so a Boolean result is clearer than an exception.

## Params

`params` lets callers provide zero or more arguments without constructing the parameter collection explicitly. C# 13 extended the feature beyond arrays to recognized collection types.

- Must be the last parameter in the method signature.
- Individual arguments or no arguments use expanded form, which constructs the declared `params` collection at the call site.
- Normal form accepts one expression implicitly convertible to the declared parameter type. An array works only when that array-to-parameter conversion exists, including the applicable array-to-span conversion.

```csharp
static int Sum(params int[] numbers)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (var n in numbers)
        total += n;
    return total;
}

Sum(1, 2, 3);   // 6
Sum();           // 0
Sum(new[] { 4, 5 }); // 9 — explicit array also works
```

C# 13 permits collection types such as `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, and types with a suitable collection-builder shape. Allocation behavior still depends on the declared parameter type and whether the call uses expanded or normal form.

```csharp
static int Sum(params ReadOnlySpan<int> numbers)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (var n in numbers)
        total += n;
    return total;
}
```

# Inheritance Method Keywords

## Virtual

`virtual` marks a base implementation as an extension point. Calls through a base reference still select the most-derived override at runtime.

- Enables runtime polymorphism.
- Calls are resolved by the runtime type, not just the variable type.

```csharp
class Animal
{
    public virtual string Speak() => "...";
}
```

## Override

`override` supplies the derived implementation of a virtual or abstract member while keeping the same dispatch slot.

- Signature must match the base member.
- The derived method can still call the base implementation with `base.MethodName()`.

```csharp
class Dog : Animal
{
    public override string Speak() => "Woof";
}
```

## New

`new` declares a separate member that hides one inherited with the same name. It does not join the base member's dispatch slot.

- Behavior depends on the compile-time type of the variable.
- `new` is appropriate only as a deliberate choice when member hiding, rather than polymorphism, is the required behavior.

```csharp
class Animal
{
    public string Category() => "Animal";
}

class Dog : Animal
{
    public new string Category() => "Dog";
}
```

## Virtual Vs Override Vs New in One Example

```csharp
class Animal
{
    public virtual string Speak() => "...";
    public string Category() => "Animal";
}

class Dog : Animal
{
    public override string Speak() => "Woof";
    public new string Category() => "Dog";
}

Animal asAnimal = new Dog();
Dog asDog = new Dog();

Console.WriteLine(asAnimal.Speak());    // Woof (runtime dispatch)
Console.WriteLine(asDog.Speak());       // Woof
Console.WriteLine(asAnimal.Category()); // Animal (member hiding)
Console.WriteLine(asDog.Category());    // Dog
```

Both objects have the same runtime type. Only the lookup rule changes: runtime type for `Speak`, compile-time reference type for `Category`.

# Other Method Forms

- **`ref return` and `ref readonly return`** return an alias to existing storage. The writable form lets a caller update that storage. The readonly form avoids a copy without granting mutation. Ref-safety rules prevent the alias from outliving its source.
- **Local functions** name behavior inside another method. A `static` local function cannot capture outer state, and a direct call needs no delegate. A lambda is the natural form when the method must produce a `Func` or `Action` value.
- **Extension methods** are static methods whose first parameter has the `this` modifier. They participate in normal static overload resolution and do not modify the extended type.
- **Expression-bodied members** use shorter syntax for a single expression. Their call and dispatch semantics do not change.

A method's signature does not include its generic constraints, and `object` and `dynamic` cannot distinguish signatures. Methods differing only in either respect are duplicate declarations, not ambiguous choices at a call site.

**Overload resolution** compares the applicable candidates and their required conversions. Optional and named arguments affect applicability, while an unresolved tie is a compile error. Modern compilers can cache some static method-group conversions, but capturing lambdas and instance targets still need their own lifetime analysis.

# Pitfalls

- Optional defaults are copied into the caller at compile time. Changing a library's default does not affect an already compiled consumer, so a default-value change can create version-dependent behavior.
- An `in` parameter does not guarantee zero copies. Conversions and non-variable arguments can require temporaries, and readonly access to a mutable struct may trigger defensive copies.
- Member hiding with `new` makes the result depend on the reference's compile-time type. That split is hard to reason about in public APIs unless compatibility requires it.

# Tradeoffs

| Decision | Option A | Option B | When A | When B |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **By-value vs `in`** | By-value copies the value | `in` passes a readonly alias | Small values and ordinary APIs | Large readonly structs on a measured hot path |
| **`in` vs `ref`** | `in` forbids reassignment through the parameter | `ref` permits it | The callee only reads | Mutation or rebinding is part of the contract |
| **`override` vs `new`** | `override` uses runtime polymorphism | `new` uses compile-time hiding | Derived behavior must work through base references | A deliberate compatibility split requires a separate member |
| **`params T[]` vs `params ReadOnlySpan<T>`** | Array form is broadly compatible and can be retained by the callee | Span form is stack-only and cannot escape | The method or caller needs array semantics | Synchronous processing benefits from span-based calls |

By-value parameters and ordinary virtual dispatch are the default. By-reference semantics fit when aliasing is part of the API or profiling shows that struct copies matter. `new` fits only when compile-time hiding is the intended contract.

# Questions

> [!qard]- How do `ref`, `out`, and `in` parameters differ?
> All three pass the argument by reference instead of copying its value. For `ref` and `out`, the parameter always aliases the caller's variable. For `in`, it aliases the caller's variable when the argument is a variable of the parameter's type. An `in` argument that is not a variable, or that needs a conversion, can instead be copied into a temporary, and the parameter then refers to that temporary. The three modifiers differ in which direction data may flow through the reference.

> | Modifier | How data flows through the reference | Typical use |
> |---|---|---|

> | `out` | Outward. The caller can pass an unassigned variable. The method cannot read it before assigning it and must assign it before every normal return | Returning an extra result, as in `Try` methods such as `Dictionary.TryGetValue` |
> | `in` | Inward and readonly. The caller must initialize the argument, and the method can read the parameter but cannot assign it | Avoiding copies of a large struct on a measured hot path |
>
> Without a modifier, the parameter is a copy, so assigning it never changes the caller's variable.
>

The method can mutate the shared object through that copy, but assigning a different object changes only its local copy. `ref` aliases the caller’s variable, allowing the method to replace the reference stored there. > [!qard]- How does C# apply an optional parameter's default value, and why can already-compiled callers keep an old default?
> The default is applied at the call site. When an ordinary compiled call omits an optional argument, the compiler inserts the declared default value into the caller's code, and the method receives it like any other argument.
>
> The declaration rules fit that mechanism:
>
> - **The default must be a compile-time value:** a constant expression, `default(S)`, or `new S()` where `S` is a value type. The compiler has to be able to write the value into each call.
> - **Optional parameters come after all required parameters.** Named arguments let a call supply a later optional argument while omitting earlier ones.
>

> [!qard]- Which modifiers on a base-class method and a same-named derived-class method make a call through a base-typed reference run the derived implementation?

> [!qard]- What does declaring a base-class method `virtual` commit that API to?

Derived classes can replace its behavior, unless an override along the hierarchy is marked `sealed`, which stops classes below it from overriding the member again. > [!qard]- A base method is not virtual, but a derived class needs different behavior. What are the options, and which ones work through a base-class reference?

>
> | Option | Call through a base reference | Fits when |
> |---|---|---|
> | Base member made `virtual`, derived member marked `override` | Runs the derived implementation, chosen by the object's runtime type | The base type can be changed and derived objects are meant to substitute for base objects |
> | Derived member declared with `new` (hiding) | Still runs the base implementation. Only references typed as the derived class reach the new member | Hiding itself is the intended behavior, such as a deliberate compatibility split, not polymorphism |
> | Composition | No inheritance dispatch is involved. The class delegates the varying step to an object it holds | The base cannot be changed, or the variation is not a natural subtype relationship |
>

> [!qard]- Can overloads differ only by `object` versus `dynamic`, or by generic constraints?

> [!qard]- Which receiver type controls extension-method lookup?
> The compile-time type controls lookup. With `Base value = new Derived()`, a method declared only on `Derived` is not found through `value`; an applicable extension for `Base` can be selected instead. An applicable instance method found by ordinary lookup takes precedence over an extension. Generic constraints determine whether an extension candidate is applicable, not whether runtime dispatch replaces it. [Microsoft: extension methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/extension-methods)

> Type inference can infer `T` as `Derived`, giving the generic candidate an identity conversion. The non-generic candidate needs a conversion from `Derived` to `Base`, so it is a worse match. The generic candidate does not win merely because its constraints are satisfied; constraints must hold for applicability, and otherwise-equivalent candidates have additional tie-breakers. An argument declared as `object` is considered as `object`, even when its runtime value is a string. [C# specification: overload resolution](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions#1264-overload-resolution)

> [!qard]- Why can adding an applicable derived overload change a call that previously used a base overload?
> Method lookup can find an applicable declaration on the derived type and exclude base declarations before the better-function-member comparison. For a derived `Process(double)` and inherited `Process(int)`, `derived.Process(5)` can select the derived member using the implicit int-to-double conversion. This is a lookup rule, not virtual dispatch or a blanket rule that every same-named derived method excludes every base member. Public overload additions can therefore change source behavior when callers recompile. [C# specification: method invocations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions#128103-method-invocations)

> [!qard]- When does a returned `ref` let a caller change the original storage?
> The caller must retain the alias with a `ref` local or another ref-aware operation. Ordinary assignment reads and copies the value instead:
>
> ```csharp
> static ref int Larger(ref int first, ref int second)
> {
>     if (first > second)
>     {
>         return ref first;
>     }
>     return ref second;
> }
>
> int a = 5;
> int b = 10;
> ref int selected = ref Larger(ref a, ref b);
> // This changes b to 100.
> selected = 100;
> ```
>
> A separate `out` assignment copies a value into its own destination; it does not create another alias to the returned storage. Ref-safety rules prevent returning storage whose lifetime is too short, such as an ordinary local that disappears when the method returns. Methods define where behavior begins and what data may cross the boundary. The parameter list is part of that contract. By-value parameters isolate the caller's variable, `ref` and `out` expose it for reassignment, and `in` exposes storage as readonly. `params` changes how an expanded argument list is collected at the call site.

Inheritance adds a separate question: which implementation runs? `virtual` and `override` use runtime dispatch. `new` hides a member and leaves selection to the compile-time type of the reference. Similar syntax, very different behavior.

# Input Parameters

## Ref

`ref` aliases the caller's storage rather than copying its current value into a new parameter variable.

- The caller must initialize the variable.
- The method can read and write the variable.

For reference types, `ref` allows the callee to replace the caller's reference rather than only mutate the referenced object:

```csharp
class MyClass {}

static void ModifyReference(ref MyClass obj)
{
    obj = new MyClass();
}

var myObj = new MyClass();
ModifyReference(ref myObj);
```

For value types, `ref` allows the callee to update the caller's variable:

```csharp
static void InitializeAndModify(ref int value)
{
    value = 10;
}

int num = 0;
InitializeAndModify(ref num);
```

## In

`in` is a readonly by-reference parameter. It can avoid copying a large struct, though the compiler may still create a temporary for argument expressions that are not variables.

- The caller must initialize the argument.
- The method can read, but cannot assign to the parameter.
- It is most useful when measurements show that copying a large readonly struct matters.

```csharp
static void ProcessData(in int value)
{
    // value = 10; // Compile-time error
    Console.WriteLine(value);
}
```

## Out

`out` also aliases caller storage, but the value flows outward. The caller need not initialize it, and every normal return path must assign it. This supports `Try*` APIs that separate success from the produced value.

```csharp
static bool TryDivide(int a, int b, out int result)
{
    if (b == 0) { result = 0; return false; }
    result = a / b;
    return true;
}

if (TryDivide(10, 2, out var quotient))   // 'quotient' declared inline
    Console.WriteLine(quotient);           // 5
```

`Dictionary.TryGetValue` shows the boundary well: a missing key is expected input, so a Boolean result is clearer than an exception.

## Params

`params` lets callers provide zero or more arguments without constructing the parameter collection explicitly. C# 13 extended the feature beyond arrays to recognized collection types.

- Must be the last parameter in the method signature.
- Individual arguments or no arguments use expanded form, which constructs the declared `params` collection at the call site.
- Normal form accepts one expression implicitly convertible to the declared parameter type. An array works only when that array-to-parameter conversion exists, including the applicable array-to-span conversion.

```csharp
static int Sum(params int[] numbers)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (var n in numbers)
        total += n;
    return total;
}

Sum(1, 2, 3);   // 6
Sum();           // 0
Sum(new[] { 4, 5 }); // 9 — explicit array also works
```

C# 13 permits collection types such as `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, and types with a suitable collection-builder shape. Allocation behavior still depends on the declared parameter type and whether the call uses expanded or normal form.

```csharp
static int Sum(params ReadOnlySpan<int> numbers)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (var n in numbers)
        total += n;
    return total;
}
```

> [Microsoft: method parameters](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/method-parameters)

<!-- qard-id: 19ea3788-056c-4ed6-8bc6-2087ae866f65 -->
> [!qard]- How does C# apply an optional parameter's default value, and why can already-compiled callers keep an old default?
> The default is applied at the call site. When an ordinary compiled call omits an optional argument, the compiler inserts the declared default value into the caller's code, and the method receives it like any other argument.
>
> The declaration rules fit that mechanism:
>
> - **The default must be a compile-time value:** a constant expression, `default(S)`, or `new S()` where `S` is a value type. The compiler has to be able to write the value into each call.
> - **Optional parameters come after all required parameters.** Named arguments let a call supply a later optional argument while omitting earlier ones.
> 
> **Versioning consequence:** the default lives in each caller's compiled code. If a library changes a default, callers compiled against the old version keep passing the old value until they are recompiled. A public default value is therefore part of the library's compatibility contract.
>
> [Microsoft: named and optional arguments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/named-and-optional-arguments) · [C#: 12.6.2.3 Run-time evaluation of argument lists](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions#12623-run-time-evaluation-of-argument-lists)

<!-- qard-id: ffd19d60-4643-4ede-92ff-83ba55b3f613 -->
> [!qard]- Which modifiers on a base-class method and a same-named derived-class method make a call through a base-typed reference run the derived implementation?
> The base method must be declared `virtual`, and the derived method must implement it with `override`. The call is then resolved by the runtime type of the object rather than by the declared type of the variable.
>
> Methods are non-virtual by default. If the base method is not virtual, a call through a base-typed variable binds to the base implementation, even when the derived class declares its own method with `new`.
>
> [Microsoft: virtual keyword](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/virtual) · [Microsoft: new modifier](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/new-modifier)

> [!qard]- What does declaring a base-class method `virtual` commit that API to?
> A virtual member is an extension point. Derived classes can replace its behavior, unless an override along the hierarchy is marked `sealed`, which stops classes below it from overriding the member again. Ordinary calls to the member on such an object run the most-derived override, including calls made from code inside the base class. An explicit call through `base` in a derived class is the exception: it runs the base class's implementation rather than the most-derived override. The base class can therefore no longer assume that its own implementation of that member is the one that runs.
>
> [Microsoft: virtual keyword](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/virtual) · [Microsoft: new modifier](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/new-modifier) · [Microsoft: base keyword](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/base) · [Microsoft: sealed modifier](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/sealed)

<!-- qard-id: 13e7573c-4ba4-4f2b-a316-4f2dcb52ccd6 -->
> [!qard]- A base method is not virtual, but a derived class needs different behavior. What are the options, and which ones work through a base-class reference?
> Only virtual dispatch makes a call through a base-class reference run derived code. Making the base member `virtual` and overriding it is therefore the only option that works through such a reference. Hiding with `new` affects only derived-typed references, and composition moves the variation out of inheritance.
>
> | Option | Call through a base reference | Fits when |
> |---|---|---|
> | Base member made `virtual`, derived member marked `override` | Runs the derived implementation, chosen by the object's runtime type | The base type can be changed and derived objects are meant to substitute for base objects |
> | Derived member declared with `new` (hiding) | Still runs the base implementation. Only references typed as the derived class reach the new member | Hiding itself is the intended behavior, such as a deliberate compatibility split, not polymorphism |
> | Composition | No inheritance dispatch is involved. The class delegates the varying step to an object it holds | The base cannot be changed, or the variation is not a natural subtype relationship |
>
> Hiding is the common trap. The same object behaves differently depending on whether it is referenced as the derived type or as the base type.
>
> [Microsoft: virtual keyword](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/virtual) · [Microsoft: new modifier](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/new-modifier)

> [!qard]- Can overloads differ only by `object` versus `dynamic`, or by generic constraints?
> No. Neither distinction gives these methods different signatures. `M(object value)` and `M(dynamic value)` collide, as do two `M<T>(T value)` declarations distinguished only by `where T : class` versus `where T : struct`. The compiler rejects the duplicate declarations before resolving any call. `dynamic` still changes binding of operations that use it; sharing this signature representation does not make its behavior identical to `object`. [C# specification: signatures and overloading](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/basic-concepts#76-signatures-and-overloading)

> [!qard]- Which receiver type controls extension-method lookup?
> The compile-time type controls lookup. With `Base value = new Derived()`, a method declared only on `Derived` is not found through `value`; an applicable extension for `Base` can be selected instead. An applicable instance method found by ordinary lookup takes precedence over an extension. Generic constraints determine whether an extension candidate is applicable, not whether runtime dispatch replaces it. [Microsoft: extension methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/extension-methods)

> [!qard]- Why can `Print<T>(T value)` beat `Print(Base value)` for an argument declared as `Derived`?
> Type inference can infer `T` as `Derived`, giving the generic candidate an identity conversion. The non-generic candidate needs a conversion from `Derived` to `Base`, so it is a worse match. The generic candidate does not win merely because its constraints are satisfied; constraints must hold for applicability, and otherwise-equivalent candidates have additional tie-breakers. An argument declared as `object` is considered as `object`, even when its runtime value is a string. [C# specification: overload resolution](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions#1264-overload-resolution)

> [!qard]- Why can adding an applicable derived overload change a call that previously used a base overload?
> Method lookup can find an applicable declaration on the derived type and exclude base declarations before the better-function-member comparison. For a derived `Process(double)` and inherited `Process(int)`, `derived.Process(5)` can select the derived member using the implicit int-to-double conversion. This is a lookup rule, not virtual dispatch or a blanket rule that every same-named derived method excludes every base member. Public overload additions can therefore change source behavior when callers recompile. [C# specification: method invocations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/expressions#128103-method-invocations)

> [!qard]- When does a returned `ref` let a caller change the original storage?
> The caller must retain the alias with a `ref` local or another ref-aware operation. Ordinary assignment reads and copies the value instead:
>
> ```csharp
> static ref int Larger(ref int first, ref int second)
> {
>     if (first > second)
>     {
>         return ref first;
>     }
>     return ref second;
> }
>
> int a = 5;
> int b = 10;
> ref int selected = ref Larger(ref a, ref b);
> // This changes b to 100.
> selected = 100;
> ```
>
> A separate `out` assignment copies a value into its own destination; it does not create another alias to the returned storage. Ref-safety rules prevent returning storage whose lifetime is too short, such as an ordinary local that disappears when the method returns. [Microsoft: ref returns and ref locals](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/jump-statements#ref-returns)

---
title: C# Types
topic: [Programming]
subtopic: [NET]
summary: "How C# types define shape, behavior, and value versus reference assignment semantics."
tags: [FolderNote]
publish: true
status: Creation
priority: Medium
level: ["4"]
qard-deck: "Programming"
qard-topic: "NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Types"
flashcard_uid: "a5c39ae2"
created: "2026-02-10T16:03:55.000Z"
modified: "2026-11-03T09:57:43.792Z"
published: "2026-07-08T13:14:17.329Z"
---

A C# type defines what values exist, which operations are valid, and what assignment copies. Value types copy their contained value. Reference types copy a reference to one object. That distinction controls aliasing and equality long before stack-versus-heap details matter.

The folder separates the main forms. Classes and record classes are reference types. Structs and record structs are value types. Strings, delegates, and events add specialized behavior on top of the same type system.

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Copy and Storage Boundaries

- **Assignment:** a value-type assignment copies every field. Reference fields inside that value still point to the same objects. A reference-type assignment copies the object reference, so both variables can observe mutations to one instance.
- **Arguments:** parameters are passed by value unless marked `ref`, `out`, or `in`. Passing a reference type by value copies the reference, not the object.
- **Storage:** a value type is stored inline in whatever holds it: a local variable, a field of a heap object, or an array element. A reference-type variable holds only a reference to an object instance, so the reference and the object are distinct. Where either physically resides is a runtime detail. Declaration kind therefore does not dictate one physical location.
- **Boxing:** conversion from a value type to `object` or an interface value copies it into a box. Constrained generic calls can often avoid that allocation. Nullable value types box differently: a populated `Nullable<T>` boxes its underlying `T` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating a box.

# Pitfalls

- **Hidden aliases.** Several references can point at one mutable object. Ownership must be clear. Shared models are easier to reason about when immutable.
- **Mutable value copies.** A property, indexer, or `foreach` variable usually exposes a struct copy. Mutation may be rejected by the compiler or affect only the copy. Readonly structs and whole-value replacement keep that boundary visible.
- **Equality chosen by accident.** Classes use reference equality unless they define another contract. Record classes and record structs synthesize value equality, while ordinary structs inherit field-based default equality. Domain identity should decide, not syntax convenience.

# Tradeoffs

- **Class or struct:** a class makes shared identity and inheritance available. A struct gives value-copy semantics and can avoid a separate allocation, but large copies and boxing may cost more.
- **Record class or conventional class:** records fit data whose contents define equality. Identity-rich entities usually need conventional class semantics.
- **Interface or constrained generic:** an interface value gives runtime polymorphism but boxes a struct. A constrained generic can preserve static typing and avoid the box.

# Examples

```csharp
var h = new Holder { Counter = new Counter { Value = 0 } };

// Property access returns a copy of the struct value.
h.Counter.Inc();
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 0

// Fix: replace the whole value after mutation.
var c = h.Counter;
c.Inc();
h.Counter = c;
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 1

public struct Counter
{
    public int Value;
    public void Inc() => Value++;
}

public sealed class Holder
{
    public Counter Counter { get; set; }
}
```

The direct `h.Counter.Inc()` call compiles, but it mutates the temporary value returned by the property and then discards that copy. A direct field assignment such as `h.Counter.Value = 1` is rejected with CS1612. Reading the value into `c`, mutating it, and assigning it back persists the change.

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: d8eb59cf-ad2d-43be-954f-44db23f34d38 -->
> [!qard]- Why might mutating a struct inside `foreach` fail to update the collection?
> In an ordinary (non-`ref`) `foreach`, each struct element reaches the loop body as a copy held in a read-only iteration variable. Changes to the copy's own fields never reach the stored element.
>
> - Assigning the iteration variable, or one of its fields, is rejected by the compiler.
> - Calling a mutating method on it compiles, but the method changes the copy's fields rather than the stored element's, so the update is silently lost.
> 
> The copy is shallow. When a field of the struct refers to an object, such as a `List<T>`, the copy and the stored element refer to the same object. A change made to that object through the copy, such as adding an item, therefore remains visible through the collection. Only changes to the struct's own field values are lost.
>
>
> An ordinary struct-valued property has a similar copy boundary: a mutating method call can change only the returned temporary. Direct field assignment through that property may instead be rejected. A property containing a struct enumerator can return a fresh copy on each access, so repeatedly calling MoveNext on the property does not advance one persistent enumerator.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

> [!qard]- How can stored struct elements be updated rather than discarded copies?
> The stored elements can be updated in two ways. The same read-modify-write-back approach applies to an ordinary struct-valued property:
>
> - **Indexed write-back:** a loop by index reads `items[i]` into a local, changes the local and assigns it back to `items[i]`, replacing the whole element value.
> - **`ref` iteration:** when the collection exposes its elements by reference, as `Span<T>` does, `foreach (ref var item in span)` makes `item` an alias for the stored element, so changes apply in place.
> 
> Mutable structs make this mistake easy. Immutable structs, updated by creating a new value and assigning it back, keep the copy boundary visible.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

<!-- qard-id: b89f32ef-f23d-488d-a26a-78ebe0051826 -->
> [!qard]- Where does boxing commonly happen?
> Boxing happens wherever a value type is converted to `object` or to an interface it implements. The runtime allocates an object on the managed heap and copies the value into it. A nullable value type is boxed according to its contents: a populated `int?` boxes its underlying `int` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating.
>
> Common places:
>
> - **`object`-typed variables, collections and parameters:** `object o = 42;`, adding an `int` to a `List<object>` or an `ArrayList`, or passing a struct to a parameter of type `object`.
> - **Interface-typed variables and parameters:** assigning a struct to an `IComparable` variable, or passing it where an interface type is declared.
> 
> Each box is a separate heap allocation that the garbage collector must later reclaim. The box also holds a copy, so later changes to the original value do not affect it.
>
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

> [!qard]- How can boxing be reduced on a measured hot path?
> The conversion to object or an interface value must be removed from the actual call path.
>
> - **Generic collections and APIs:** a generic collection such as `List<int>` is specialized for `int`, so adding an element stores the value without converting it to `object`.
> - **Constrained generics instead of interface-typed parameters:** a method such as `Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>` can call `CompareTo` on a struct argument without converting it to the interface type, provided the struct itself implements that member.
> 
> These changes matter mainly in frequently executed code. They justify extra API complexity where profiling shows boxing allocations are significant.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

<!-- qard-id: d5bda60c-1799-4e4a-ab36-7624ae085e3a -->
> [!qard]- When should a type be a `struct`, `class`, or `record class`?
> The choice follows the semantics the type needs. A `struct` fits a small value that is copied field by field, a `class` fits an object with its own identity, and a `record class` fits a reference type whose contents define its equality. Copying, mutation and measured allocation costs then confirm or adjust that semantic choice.
>
> | Aspect | `struct` | `class` | `record class` |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Assignment and passing | Copies every field, so each variable holds its own field values. The copy is shallow: a reference-type field copies only the reference, so both copies can still point to one object. | Copies a reference, so several variables can share and observe one object. | Copies a reference, as a class does. |
> | Default equality | `Equals` is true when both have the same type and the same stored values. | Equality holds only when both references point to the same object, even if every field matches. | Compiler-generated `Equals` and `==` compare the type and member values. The generated `GetHashCode` compares nothing; it returns hash codes compatible with that equality, so equal records hash equally. |
> | Mutation | A change to a copy's own fields affects only that copy, so such changes are easy to lose. A change to an object reached through a reference field is visible through every copy that shares it. | A change is visible through every reference to the object. | Positional properties are init-only by default, and a `with` expression creates a modified shallow copy whose reference-type members still point to the same objects. |
> | Allocation and cost | Stored inline in the variable, field or array element that holds it, with no allocation of its own. Large values make every copy expensive, and boxing allocates. | One heap allocation per instance. | One heap allocation per instance, as with a class. |
> | Inheritance | Cannot derive from another struct or class or serve as a base type, though it can implement interfaces. | Supports class inheritance. | Can inherit only from another record. |
> | Typical fit | Small data-centric values with little behavior, such as a coordinate. | Entities with identity, a lifecycle or polymorphic behavior. | Data defined by its contents, such as messages or DTOs. |
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types) · [Microsoft Learn: Classes (C# language specification)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes) · [Microsoft Learn: Records](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record)

> [!qard]- Why can two anonymous objects compare unequal with `==` but match in `Intersect`?
> Anonymous types synthesize value-based `Equals` and `GetHashCode`, but do not overload `==`; that operator compares reference identity. Two separately created anonymous objects with the same property names, types, order, and values in the same assembly therefore compare unequal with `==` but equal with `Equals`. `Intersect` uses the default equality comparer, which uses their generated equality and hash rather than the `==` operator. Each property is compared with its own type's equality, not recursively by arbitrary object contents. [Microsoft: anonymous types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/anonymous-types)

# References

- [C# type system](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/)

notes.content:
---
title: C# Types
topic: [Programming]
subtopic: [NET]
summary: "How C# types define shape, behavior, and value versus reference assignment semantics."
tags: [FolderNote]
publish: true
status: Creation
priority: Medium
level: ["4"]
qard-deck: "Programming"
qard-topic: "NET/CSharp/Fundamentals/Types/Types"
flashcard_uid: "a5c39ae2"
created: "2026-02-10T16:03:55.000Z"
modified: "2026-11-03T09:57:43.792Z"
published: "2026-07-08T13:14:17.329Z"
---

A C# type defines what values exist, which operations are valid, and what assignment copies. Value types copy their contained value. Reference types copy a reference to one object. That distinction controls aliasing and equality long before stack-versus-heap details matter.

The folder separates the main forms. Classes and record classes are reference types. Structs and record structs are value types. Strings, delegates, and events add specialized behavior on top of the same type system.

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Copy and Storage Boundaries

- **Assignment:** a value-type assignment copies every field. Reference fields inside that value still point to the same objects. A reference-type assignment copies the object reference, so both variables can observe mutations to one instance.
- **Arguments:** parameters are passed by value unless marked `ref`, `out`, or `in`. Passing a reference type by value copies the reference, not the object.
- **Storage:** a value type is stored inline in whatever holds it: a local variable, a field of a heap object, or an array element. A reference-type variable holds only a reference to an object instance, so the reference and the object are distinct. Where either physically resides is a runtime detail. Declaration kind therefore does not dictate one physical location.
- **Boxing:** conversion from a value type to `object` or an interface value copies it into a box. Constrained generic calls can often avoid that allocation. Nullable value types box differently: a populated `Nullable<T>` boxes its underlying `T` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating a box.

# Pitfalls

- **Hidden aliases.** Several references can point at one mutable object. Ownership must be clear. Shared models are easier to reason about when immutable.
- **Mutable value copies.** A property, indexer, or `foreach` variable usually exposes a struct copy. Mutation may be rejected by the compiler or affect only the copy. Readonly structs and whole-value replacement keep that boundary visible.
- **Equality chosen by accident.** Classes use reference equality unless they define another contract. Record classes and record structs synthesize value equality, while ordinary structs inherit field-based default equality. Domain identity should decide, not syntax convenience.

# Tradeoffs

- **Class or struct:** a class makes shared identity and inheritance available. A struct gives value-copy semantics and can avoid a separate allocation, but large copies and boxing may cost more.
- **Record class or conventional class:** records fit data whose contents define equality. Identity-rich entities usually need conventional class semantics.
- **Interface or constrained generic:** an interface value gives runtime polymorphism but boxes a struct. A constrained generic can preserve static typing and avoid the box.

# Examples

```csharp
var h = new Holder { Counter = new Counter { Value = 0 } };

// Property access returns a copy of the struct value.
h.Counter.Inc();
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 0

// Fix: replace the whole value after mutation.
var c = h.Counter;
c.Inc();
h.Counter = c;
Console.WriteLine(h.Counter.Value); // 1

public struct Counter
{
    public int Value;
    public void Inc() => Value++;
}

public sealed class Holder
{
    public Counter Counter { get; set; }
}
```

The direct `h.Counter.Inc()` call compiles, but it mutates the temporary value returned by the property and then discards that copy. A direct field assignment such as `h.Counter.Value = 1` is rejected with CS1612. Reading the value into `c`, mutating it, and assigning it back persists the change.

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: d8eb59cf-ad2d-43be-954f-44db23f34d38 -->
> [!qard]- Why might mutating a struct inside `foreach` fail to update the collection?
> In an ordinary (non-`ref`) `foreach`, each struct element reaches the loop body as a copy held in a read-only iteration variable. Changes to the copy's own fields never reach the stored element.
>
> - Assigning the iteration variable, or one of its fields, is rejected by the compiler.
> - Calling a mutating method on it compiles, but the method changes the copy's fields rather than the stored element's, so the update is silently lost.
> 
> The copy is shallow. When a field of the struct refers to an object, such as a `List<T>`, the copy and the stored element refer to the same object. A change made to that object through the copy, such as adding an item, therefore remains visible through the collection. Only changes to the struct's own field values are lost.
>
>
> An ordinary struct-valued property has a similar copy boundary: a mutating method call can change only the returned temporary. Direct field assignment through that property may instead be rejected. A property containing a struct enumerator can return a fresh copy on each access, so repeatedly calling MoveNext on the property does not advance one persistent enumerator.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

> [!qard]- How can stored struct elements be updated rather than discarded copies?
> The stored elements can be updated in two ways. The same read-modify-write-back approach applies to an ordinary struct-valued property:
>
> - **Indexed write-back:** a loop by index reads `items[i]` into a local, changes the local and assigns it back to `items[i]`, replacing the whole element value.
> - **`ref` iteration:** when the collection exposes its elements by reference, as `Span<T>` does, `foreach (ref var item in span)` makes `item` an alias for the stored element, so changes apply in place.
> 
> Mutable structs make this mistake easy. Immutable structs, updated by creating a new value and assigning it back, keep the copy boundary visible.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Iteration statements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/statements/iteration-statements) · [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types)

<!-- qard-id: b89f32ef-f23d-488d-a26a-78ebe0051826 -->
> [!qard]- Where does boxing commonly happen?
> Boxing happens wherever a value type is converted to `object` or to an interface it implements. The runtime allocates an object on the managed heap and copies the value into it. A nullable value type is boxed according to its contents: a populated `int?` boxes its underlying `int` value, and an empty one converts to a `null` reference without allocating.
>
> Common places:
>
> - **`object`-typed variables, collections and parameters:** `object o = 42;`, adding an `int` to a `List<object>` or an `ArrayList`, or passing a struct to a parameter of type `object`.
> - **Interface-typed variables and parameters:** assigning a struct to an `IComparable` variable, or passing it where an interface type is declared.
> 
> Each box is a separate heap allocation that the garbage collector must later reclaim. The box also holds a copy, so later changes to the original value do not affect it.
>
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

> [!qard]- How can boxing be reduced on a measured hot path?
> The conversion to object or an interface value must be removed from the actual call path.
>
> - **Generic collections and APIs:** a generic collection such as `List<int>` is specialized for `int`, so adding an element stores the value without converting it to `object`.
> - **Constrained generics instead of interface-typed parameters:** a method such as `Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>` can call `CompareTo` on a struct argument without converting it to the interface type, provided the struct itself implements that member.
> 
> These changes matter mainly in frequently executed code. They justify extra API complexity where profiling shows boxing allocations are significant.
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Boxing and unboxing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/types/boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Nullable value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/nullable-value-types#boxing-and-unboxing) · [Microsoft Learn: Generic classes and methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/generics) · [Microsoft Learn: OpCodes.Constrained](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.emit.opcodes.constrained?view=net-10.0)

<!-- qard-id: d5bda60c-1799-4e4a-ab36-7624ae085e3a -->
> [!qard]- When should a type be a `struct`, `class`, or `record class`?
> The choice follows the semantics the type needs. A `struct` fits a small value that is copied field by field, a `class` fits an object with its own identity, and a `record class` fits a reference type whose contents define its equality. Copying, mutation and measured allocation costs then confirm or adjust that semantic choice.
>
> | Aspect | `struct` | `class` | `record class` |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Assignment and passing | Copies every field, so each variable holds its own field values. The copy is shallow: a reference-type field copies only the reference, so both copies can still point to one object. | Copies a reference, so several variables can share and observe one object. | Copies a reference, as a class does. |
> | Default equality | `Equals` is true when both have the same type and the same stored values. | Equality holds only when both references point to the same object, even if every field matches. | Compiler-generated `Equals` and `==` compare the type and member values. The generated `GetHashCode` compares nothing; it returns hash codes compatible with that equality, so equal records hash equally. |
> | Mutation | A change to a copy's own fields affects only that copy, so such changes are easy to lose. A change to an object reached through a reference field is visible through every copy that shares it. | A change is visible through every reference to the object. | Positional properties are init-only by default, and a `with` expression creates a modified shallow copy whose reference-type members still point to the same objects. |
> | Allocation and cost | Stored inline in the variable, field or array element that holds it, with no allocation of its own. Large values make every copy expensive, and boxing allocates. | One heap allocation per instance. | One heap allocation per instance, as with a class. |
> | Inheritance | Cannot derive from another struct or class or serve as a base type, though it can implement interfaces. | Supports class inheritance. | Can inherit only from another record. |
> | Typical fit | Small data-centric values with little behavior, such as a coordinate. | Entities with identity, a lifecycle or polymorphic behavior. | Data defined by its contents, such as messages or DTOs. |
>
> Sources: [Microsoft Learn: Structure types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/struct) · [Microsoft Learn: Value types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types) · [Microsoft Learn: Classes (C# language specification)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/language-specification/classes) · [Microsoft Learn: Records](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record)

> [!qard]- Why can two anonymous objects compare unequal with `==` but match in `Intersect`?
> Anonymous types synthesize value-based `Equals` and `GetHashCode`, but do not overload `==`; that operator compares reference identity. Two separately created anonymous objects with the same property names, types, order, and values in the same assembly therefore compare unequal with `==` but equal with `Equals`. `Intersect` uses the default equality comparer, which uses their generated equality and hash rather than the `==` operator. Each property is compared with its own type's equality, not recursively by arbitrary object contents. [Microsoft: anonymous types](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/anonymous-types)

# References

- [C# type system](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/types/)
